Arthur Okun observó en 1962 que el paro: Arthur Okun observed in 1962 that unemployment and growth go hand in hand: if GDP grows faster than its potential pace (the one allowed by population and productivity), unemployment falls, and if it grows less, it rises, even though GDP increases. In changes, $Δu = −β (g − g_p)$. The coefficient β varies from country to country: in Spain unemployment reacts strongly to the business cycle.
En niveles, la ley dice que cada punto d: In levels, the law says that each point of unemployment above the natural rate costs about c points of GDP: $(Y − Y_p)/Y_p = −c (u − u_n)$. The natural rate of unemployment is what remains when the economy is at its potential (frictional and structural unemployment); anything above that is cyclical unemployment.
William Phillips vio en 1958 que en el R: William Phillips saw in 1958 that in the United Kingdom, with low unemployment, wages rose faster. Friedman and Phelps added expectations: $π = π^e − α (u − u_n) + s$. In the short run unemployment can be lowered with more inflation, but when people expect that inflation the curve shifts: in the long run it is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment (the NAIRU). A supply shock (s), like the 1973 oil shock, raises unemployment and inflation at the same time: stagflation.
